segments.text: Imagine a robot turning at a crossroads. It makes a quarter turn, then a half turn. How could we describe each turn accurately?
Today we are learning to recognize and compare angles as turns.
Our learning goal is to recognize and compare angles as turns.
Success criteria identify vertices and arms classify angles and compare degrees.
An angle is the amount of turning between two rays meeting at a vertex. The length of the rays does not change the angle.
A full turn is 360 degrees. A half turn is 180 and a quarter turn is 90.
Look at this angle. Is it acute? Right up to us or straight. Bose for 5 seconds and decide.
60 degrees is smaller than 90 degrees. So this is an acute angle.
A right angle is 90 degrees. It looks like the corner of a square.
An angle is 120 degrees. Is it acute or obduce? Compare it with 90 degrees.
120 is greater than 90 and less than 180. So the angle is up to us.
An angle with longer arms is not necessarily larger. We measure the amount of turning, not the length of the lines.
When measuring with a protractor, place the center at the vertex and align one arm with the zero degree baseline.
If the angle looks narrower than a right angle, should you read 75 or 105 degrees?
75 degrees is the sensible measurement because it is less than 90 degrees.
Always check which protractors scale begins at zero along your starting arm. The two scales count in opposite directions.
two adjacent angles lie on a straight line. One is 40 degrees. What is the other angle?
A straight angle is 180 degrees. Subtract 40 to get 140 degrees.
To draw an angle, draw the first way, mark the required number of degrees from 0 and connect the mark to the vertex.
A robot makes two quarter turns in the same direction. How many degrees has it turned altogether?
90 plus 90 equals 180 degrees which is a half turn.
Angles are measured in degrees, not centimeters. A small drawing and a large drawing can show exactly the same turn.
Imagine a door opening. A small opening makes an acute angle. While a door opens square to the wall makes a right angle.
A turn of 30 degrees is one third of a right angle. Three such turns add up to 90 degrees.
A turn of 150 degrees is close to a straight angle, but 30 degrees short of 180.
Use benchmarks to estimate, compare the angle with 90 degrees before reading a protractor scale.
If your measurement says 40 degrees, but the drawing looks wider than a right angle, check whether you used the wrong scale.
When drawing an angle, keep the ruler steady and make sure both rays begin at the same vertex.
Explain your answer using the size of the turn. This is stronger than simply saying the angle looks big.
Imagine a compass needle pointing north. When it rotates to east, it has completed a quarter done, even if the needle itself is very short.
If the compass turns from north to south, it has completed a half turn. The direction changed by 180 degrees.
A turn of 45 degrees is half of a right angle. We can compare it with the corner of a square to estimated size.
An angle of 80 degrees is acute even though it is almost a right angle. The exact boundary is 90 degrees.
An angle of 91 degrees is up to, even though it looks very close to a right angle. Mathematically, categories use precise boundaries.
Try drawing two rays with a narrow opening. Then rotate one ray without changing its length. Notice how the angle grows.
The vertex is the common endpoint. If the rays do not meet at the same point, we cannot identify the angle in the usual way.
Imagine a skateboarder changing direction by 135 degrees. Explain why this turn is obtuse rather than straight.
Explain the steps to someone else. Estimate the angle, align the baseline, read the correct scale and check the angle type.
Your challenge is to find three angles in your classroom, classify them and explain your reasoning.
